additive_detail:
# codes (comma separated)|what it is|what it is for|concerns|found in
E102|A synthetic yellow azo dye (tartrazine).|Colours food bright yellow.|The Southampton study linked it, mixed with other dyes and a preservative, to more hyperactivity in some children. The EU requires a warning label. A small number of people react with hives or asthma.|Lollies, soft drinks, cordial, custard powder, chips, sauces.
E104,E110,E122,E124,E129|Synthetic dyes from the azo and related families (quinoline yellow, sunset yellow, carmoisine, ponceau 4R, allura red).|Add or restore bright colour.|Same Southampton-study concern as tartrazine for children's behaviour, and the EU child-warning label applies. Some people are sensitive to azo dyes.|Lollies, drinks, sweets, flavoured snacks, desserts.
E107,E123,E151,E155|Other synthetic azo-type dyes (yellow 2G, amaranth, brilliant black BN, brown HT).|Colour.|Same child-behaviour and sensitivity concern as other azo dyes. Amaranth has been banned in the USA since the 1970s over cancer concerns.|Sweets, drinks, sauces, desserts.
E120|Carmine (cochineal), a red dye made from crushed insects.|Natural-looking red or pink colour.|Not vegetarian or vegan. Rarely causes serious allergic reactions in sensitive people.|Yoghurts, drinks, sweets, red and pink foods.
E127|Erythrosine, a synthetic red dye.|Red and pink colour.|Contains iodine and can affect the thyroid at high intake. Restricted in some countries.|Glace cherries, sweets, icing.
E132,E133|Synthetic blue dyes (indigo carmine, brilliant blue FCF).|Blue and green colour.|Generally regarded as low risk at permitted levels. A few studies in animals and cells raise questions, but evidence in people is limited.|Lollies, drinks, ice cream, icing.
E141,E153,E172|Chlorophyllins, vegetable carbon and iron oxides.|Green, black, red and brown colour.|Low concern.|Confectionery, sauces, cheese rinds.
E150,E150a,E150b,E150c,E150d|Caramel colour, made by heating sugars. The four types differ by what is added during heating.|Brown colour and mild flavour.|Types III and IV are made with ammonia, which can leave small amounts of 4-MEI, a possible carcinogen at high doses. Type I (plain) has no ammonia or sulphite.|Cola, sauces, soy sauce, gravy, biscuits, bread, beer.
E160b|Annatto, a natural orange-yellow colour from seeds.|Colour for cheese, snacks and spreads.|Natural, but can trigger allergic-type reactions, including hives, in a few sensitive people.|Cheese, butter, popcorn, snacks, custard.
E171|Titanium dioxide, a white mineral pigment.|Whitens and brightens food.|The EU banned it as a food additive in 2022 because it could not rule out genotoxic effects (damage to DNA) from the nanoparticles. Still allowed in some other countries.|Lollies, chewing gum, white icing, some supplements.
E200,E201,E202,E203|Sorbic acid and its salts (sorbates).|Stops mould and yeast, extends shelf life.|Considered low risk at permitted levels. A few people get skin irritation.|Cheese, wine, baked goods, dried fruit, drinks.
E210,E211,E212,E213|Benzoic acid and its salts (benzoates).|Preservative in acidic foods.|Can form benzene, a carcinogen, in drinks that also contain vitamin C. Linked in the Southampton study to hyperactivity in some children. Can worsen asthma or hives in sensitive people.|Soft drinks, cordial, pickles, sauces, jams.
E214,E218|Parabens (ethyl and methyl paraben), preservatives.|Stop mould and bacteria.|Weak hormone-like activity in lab studies; regulators consider low doses safe. Rarely used in food today.|Some sauces, confectionery, medicines, cosmetics.
E220,E221,E222,E223,E224,E226,E227,E228|Sulphur dioxide and sulphites.|Preserve colour, stop browning, kill microbes.|Can trigger asthma attacks and other reactions in sulphite-sensitive people, which is why it must be declared as an allergen. Destroys part of vitamin B1.|Wine, dried fruit, juices, sausages, some potato products.
E249,E250,E251,E252|Nitrites and nitrates, curing salts.|Keep cured meat pink and stop dangerous bacteria like botulism.|Nitrite can form nitrosamines in the body and in high-heat cooking, and these are linked to bowel cancer. The WHO classes processed meat as carcinogenic to humans, and nitrite curing is part of that concern.|Bacon, ham, salami, sausages, some cheese.
E280,E281,E282,E283|Propionic acid and propionates.|Stop mould, mainly in bread.|Low risk. A small trial linked calcium propionate to irritability and sleep problems in some children, but the evidence is thin.|Bread, baked goods, cheese.
E310,E311,E312,E319|Synthetic antioxidants (gallates and TBHQ).|Stop fats and oils going rancid.|Allowed only in small amounts. High doses harm animals; the amounts allowed in food are well below that, but long-term human evidence is limited.|Fried and frozen foods, instant noodles, crackers, oils.
E320,E321|BHA and BHT, synthetic antioxidants.|Stop fats going rancid.|BHA is classed as possibly carcinogenic to humans (IARC group 2B), based on animal studies. Both show weak hormone-like activity in lab studies. Permitted at low levels.|Chips, cereals, chewing gum, instant noodles, fats.
E338,E339,E340,E341,E450,E451,E452|Phosphoric acid and phosphates.|Acidity, texture, moisture holding, raising agent.|High phosphate intake is linked to kidney and bone problems, especially in people with kidney disease. Many foods add phosphate, so it can add up.|Cola, processed meat, processed cheese, baked goods.
E407|Carrageenan, a seaweed extract.|Thickens and stabilises.|Food-grade carrageenan is approved, but lab and animal studies suggest it may inflame the gut in some people. Evidence in humans is not settled.|Ice cream, plant milks, yoghurt, deli meats, desserts.
E433|Polysorbate 80, an emulsifier.|Keeps oil and water mixed.|Mouse studies suggest emulsifiers like this can disturb gut bacteria and promote gut inflammation. Human evidence is still limited.|Ice cream, sauces, baked goods, supplements.
E466|Carboxymethyl cellulose (cellulose gum).|Thickener and texture.|Mouse and small human studies suggest it may disturb gut bacteria. Considered safe by regulators at current use.|Ice cream, sauces, gluten-free baking, drinks.
E471,E472a,E472b,E472c,E472e,E481,E482|Mono- and diglycerides and related emulsifiers.|Smooth texture, longer shelf life, softer bread.|Generally low concern. They may contain small amounts of trans fat, which is not always shown on the label.|Bread, margarine, ice cream, biscuits, cakes.
E621,E622,E623,E624,E625,E620|MSG (monosodium glutamate) and related glutamates.|Savoury flavour (umami).|Regulators consider it safe. Some people report headaches or flushing after a lot of it, but controlled studies have not reliably shown this.|Instant noodles, chips, stock, sauces, takeaway.
E627,E631,E635|Flavour enhancers (guanylates, inosinates, ribonucleotides).|Boost savoury flavour, usually together with MSG.|Low concern for most people. They contain purines, so they are a poor choice for gout.|Instant noodles, chips, soups, sauces.
E950,E951,E952,E954,E955,E960,E961,E962|Intense sweeteners (acesulfame K, aspartame, cyclamate, saccharin, sucralose, steviol glycosides, neotame).|Sweeten with almost no calories.|Aspartame was classed as possibly carcinogenic (IARC group 2B) in 2023, though the JECFA expert committee kept its daily limit unchanged. It must be avoided in phenylketonuria. Some studies link sweeteners to changed gut bacteria and appetite.|Diet drinks, sugar-free lollies, yoghurt, protein products.
E965,E966,E967,E968,E420,E421,E953|Sugar alcohols (maltitol, lactitol, xylitol, erythritol, sorbitol, mannitol, isomalt).|Sweeten with fewer calories.|Can cause gas, bloating and diarrhoea in amounts as small as 10 to 20 g. Xylitol is toxic to dogs. A 2023 study linked high blood erythritol to heart attack and stroke risk; that is not yet confirmed.|Sugar-free gum, lollies, low-sugar bars, protein products.
E551,E552,E553a,E553b,E554,E556|Silicon dioxide, silicates and talc.|Anti-caking agents that keep powders flowing.|Low concern. Talc and aluminium silicates are mined minerals, so purity matters.|Salt, spices, powdered mixes, grated cheese.
E904|Shellac, a resin from the lac insect.|Glossy coating on sweets.|Not vegetarian. Low concern otherwise.|Glazed lollies, chocolates, some tablets and fruit.
E1422,E1442,E1450|Chemically modified starches.|Thicken, stabilise and survive heating and freezing.|Low concern; they are digested like starch.|Sauces, soups, pie fillings, frozen meals.
E1200|Polydextrose, a bulking fibre.|Replaces sugar and fat bulk.|Can cause gas or a laxative effect in large amounts.|Sugar-free and low-fat foods.
E541|Sodium aluminium phosphate, a raising agent.|Gives rise in baked goods.|Contains aluminium; high intake over time is a concern for some people.|Self-raising flour, cakes, pastries.
E385|Calcium disodium EDTA, a metal-binding agent.|Protects colour and flavour.|Low concern at permitted levels, but it can reduce absorption of some minerals.|Sauces, canned beans, dressings.
E461,E463,E464,E468|Cellulose-based thickeners.|Thicken and hold moisture.|Low concern. Act like fibre and can cause gas in large amounts.|Sauces, gluten-free foods, frozen foods.
E413,E415,E416,E425,E402,E404,E405|Natural gums and thickeners (tragacanth, xanthan, karaya, konjac, alginates).|Thicken and gel.|Low concern. Can cause gas or bloating in large amounts.|Sauces, dressings, desserts, gluten-free foods.
E432,E435,E436,E491,E492,E493,E494,E495|Polysorbates and sorbitan esters, emulsifiers.|Keep mixes smooth and stable.|Low concern at permitted amounts; polysorbate 80 has the most debate over gut effects.|Baked goods, ice cream, margarine.
E234,E235|Nisin and natamycin, natural preservatives.|Stop bacteria (nisin) or mould (natamycin).|Low concern.|Cheese, processed cheese, sausages.
